hook_text: In 1959, a group of young activists walked out of the ANC and set themselves a deadline: freedom by 1963.
clip_script: The 1950s. Across Africa, flags are coming down. Ghana is free in 1957. Seventeen more countries will be free in 1960. In South Africa, young Africanists are impatient. They believe Africans must lead their own liberation. They reject the words that South Africa belongs to all who live in it, black and white. The land, they say, was taken by conquest. In 1958, they break away. On 6 April 1959, in Orlando, Soweto, they launch the Pan Africanist Congress. Their president is Robert Sobukwe, a gentle university lecturer the students call Prof. Their slogan: Izwe Lethu. Our land. Their plan: on 21 March 1960, men will leave their passes at home and walk to police stations to be arrested. Nobody knows what is coming.
visual_style: Ghana's independence celebrations in 1957; a map of Africa with countries lighting up; a crowded hall in Orlando; a portrait of Robert Sobukwe; the PAC flag with a map of Africa and a gold star; a pass book left on a table.
mood: Energetic and hopeful, with a hint of foreboding.
pacing: Fast across Africa, steady at the founding, slowing to a tense finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to learn why the PAC was formed and what it stood for.
